newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Britain contemplates imperial past.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Britain contemplates imperial past.

text.p: One hundred years ago the British Empire's 400 million subjects around the world celebrated Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee with pomp and circumstance.

The Queen Empress pardoned 19,000 Indian prisoners, Sydney's paupers were given a good meal and the foundation stone was laid for Cape Town's Victoria hospital. Her 60-year reign sparked worldwide celebrations.

A century later, the sun is finally setting on Britain's colony of Hong Kong. Its handover to China on June 30 will leave Britain with a dozen dependent territories that are home to a total of 180,000 people.

These range from 58 Pitcairn Island descendants of the Bounty mutineers to the 60,000 people on the Atlantic island of Bermuda, ranked by the World Bank as one of the five richest places in the world.
Long gone are the days when Britons colonised with missionary zeal, painted the remotest corners of the globe pink and fervently believed they were bringing civilisation to grateful natives.
POST-IMPERIALIST BRITAIN "PUNCHES ABOVE ITS WEIGHT"
But to modern-day critics, the days of Empire were shameful days when Britain plundered Third World resources, traded in slaves and shipped opium to China. White might was always right.
Former U.S. Secretary of State Dean Acheson once bluntly reflected in 1962 that "Great Britain has lost an Empire but not yet found a role."

But post-imperialist Britain has sought to "punch above its weight" on the international stage with its U.N. Security Council seat, active international peacekeeping role, at times stormy involvement in the European Community and close ties with Washington.
And now the handover of Hong Kong has provoked much reflection about the legacies of Empire with diplomats and academics alike arguing there is much to be proud of.

Sir Robin McLaren, former British ambassador to Beijing who helped to negotiate Hong Kong's handover, said: "You look at the United Nations today and something between a quarter and a third are former British territories.
"For a medium-sized power like us that is quite something to reflect on. Some of these territories have been mightily successful like Malaysia and Singapore."
SHRINKING EMPIRE A FINANCIAL BURDEN ON TAXPAYER
The obligations of history have left Britain with plenty of modern-day headaches and the shrinking empire is certainly a financial burden on the taxpayer.
Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher went to war in 1982 to oust an Argentine invasion force from the Falklands, whose 2,000 islanders fervently want to stay British.
The 2,000-strong garrison, with one soldier for every islander, now costs Britain 70 million pounds a year though a long hoped for oil bonanza could sharply reduce the bill.
Rock of Gibraltar residents are constantly at loggerheads with Spain.
Pensions for Spanish workers shut out of Gibraltar when the border was closed in 1969 will cost about 140 million pounds over the next 30 years, the National Audit Office calculated.
The dwindling empire is certainly not run at a profit with British aid since the start of the 1990s totalling 153 million pounds, the office said.
Chile and Argentina lay claim to the British Antarctic Territory where penguins, not humans, reign supreme.
St Helena, where Napoleon was banished, was hit by unrest over its 20 percent unemployment rate. Caribbean territories grapple with money laundering and drug trafficking.
As historian Donald Cameron Watt of the London School of Economics put it: "The real problem with these areas is what the hell can you do with them. You cannot abandon them."
"The residue of empire is the cards which we dealt for a different game a long time ago -- but they are still on the table," he said.
BRITAIN LEAVES HONG KONG PROSPEROUS AND STABLE
George Segal, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said: "Britain can take enormous pride in Hong Kong."

"Never before has colonial rule ended with such prosperity and so rich a civil society. For this reason alone, Hong Kong's prospects, at least in the short term, are good," he wrote in the International Herald Tribune.
The handover of Hong Kong to China will reduce Britain's colonies by about 70 percent with Bermuda, which rejected independence in a referendum, the largest remaining one in terms of population.
The British have over the past half century been quick to scent the winds of change and been praised by historians for negotiating an orderly departure from their colonies.
The Hong Kong handover prompted the Daily Telegraph newspaper to launch a major review of the halcyon days when "Britannia ruled the waves and Britain never, never, never shall be slaves."
Defence Editor John Keegan, introducing the imperialist tour d'horizon, argued that the British were altruistic colonial guardians unlike Portugal and France.
"Both those ex-empires are abodes of darkness, riven by warlordism, civil war, ideological terror and dreadful human suffering.

"The old British Empire is a region of prosperous and peaceful states, ruled by legitimate governments. India is the largest democracy in the world, South Africa the largest democracy on the continent. Singapore is the seat of one of the world's most dynamic economies and Malaysia would qualify to join the European Union."
